cannot_tell.text: The studies measured their effects three or more years after each reform. The model places that effect inside 2027–2031, the law's first five years. Much of a real law's effect may come after 2031, so the yearly path is the least certain part of these numbers.

trace.part: Bus and train stops, and how often buses come
trace.text: Stop locations from the federal National Transit Map; frequencies from each agency's own schedule file or, for Madison, its published route descriptions.
2020 census homes in blocks whose centre lies within the distance: 313,564 homes in the main case.
Each place's share of the shared all-housing baseline (Census building permits, 2023–2025 average, with Milwaukee's apartments from its property file), times its share of homes near stops.
Each scenario's share of station-area homes comes from a published study of a whole city's net effect (Los Angeles, 1,136 US cities, Auckland), divided by the study's coverage where it reports one.

trace.part: That those results carry over to Wisconsin
trace.text: No Wisconsin outcome has tested the sizing. Milwaukee's and Madison's shares of homes near stops (68% and 63%) are close to Los Angeles's 61% coverage.
The little and typical responses follow the build-up measured after the New York rezonings; the strong response follows Auckland's own yearly pattern.

trace.part: Where homes land in Milwaukee and Madison
trace.text: From the cities' coded zoning: the extra floor area the law allows on each piece of land. These two cities get 41% of the typical response.

trace.part: Where homes land in the suburbs
trace.text: Zoning is not coded, so the room for new homes is estimated from existing buildings and scaled by 0.719, the ratio measured in Milwaukee and Madison. The suburbs get 59% of the typical response.
Each place's numbers are split across districts as its detached homes are (the ADU district crosswalk), not by homes near stops.
